short_form_posts.body: When you need predictable zero-token cost for agent testing and script automation, Ollama exposes a standard REST API daemon right on localhost. Integrate it into your existing Python or Node workflows without sending prompts to remote clouds.

short_form_posts.headline: Hardware Sizing 101: How to pick the right model for your VRAM.
short_form_posts.body: 7B Q4 models typically need ~4-5GB VRAM, while 14B models need ~8-10GB. If your model exceeds GPU memory, inference falls back to slower CPU compute. Sizing upfront keeps your local token generation fast and predictable.

long_form_post.title: Architecting Local AI Workflows: Why Developers Run Models on Localhost

sections.subheading: 1. The Setup Friction in Local Open-Weight Inference
sections.text: For years, running models locally meant downloading raw GGUF weights, cloning repositories, and manually configuring C++ compilers and CUDA backends. Ollama abstracts this complexity into a single background daemon and CLI across macOS, Linux, and Windows (EVID-WEB-893338BD, EVID-FORUM-F119C750).

Rather than confining models to an interactive CLI, Ollama exposes a background HTTP REST API on port 11434. Developers can query models via standard JSON payloads, making local testing an drop-in component for local development pipelines (EVID-WEB-2BAE59D7).

Local model execution is fundamentally bound by physical hardware. A quantized 7B parameter model requires approximately 4-5GB of GPU VRAM, while 14B models require 8-10GB. Ensuring adequate GPU memory avoids slow CPU fallback compute and maintains responsive token streaming (EVID-WEB-2BAE59D7, CONF-40334167).

long_form_post.cta: Get started with Ollama and explore open-weight model orchestration locally.
